subModules.title: Reading Mission: A Better Product Demo
subModules.grammarFocus: Comparative and superlative adjectives with modifiers
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Product features, performance, price, and value

content.summary: In this reading mission, you will read a short product demo about a business app. You will learn how a presenter explains product benefits, compares features with other options, and gives clear examples. You will also practise noticing how words such as far and slightly change the strength of a comparison.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Use far, much, and significantly before comparative adjectives to show a large difference. Use slightly, a little, and a bit to show a small difference. Use by far or easily with a superlative to make a strong claim.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Words and phrases for product benefits, performance, price, customer needs, and business growth.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim the passage first to understand its main purpose. Then scan for product features, comparison words, numbers, and examples that support the presenter’s claims.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short product demo about a business app.
Locate details about its speed, price, setup, and ability to support a growing team.
Recognize comparative and superlative adjectives with strength modifiers.
Identify examples that support a product’s value proposition.

contextWarmup.prompt: When choosing an app for a small business, which detail would help you make a decision?
options: A clear comparison of its price and useful features
A long list of technical words with no examples
A promise that it is the best without any evidence
contextWarmup.explanation: A clear comparison helps customers understand what they get for the price. Examples also make product claims easier to check.

rules: Use far, much, or significantly before a comparative adjective to describe a large difference: The new app is far faster than the old one.
Use slightly, a little, or a bit before a comparative adjective to describe a small difference: This plan is slightly cheaper than the other plan.
Use by far or easily before the to strengthen a superlative: It is by far the easiest system to use.

commonTrap.explanation: Do not use a strength modifier with a base adjective instead of a comparative adjective. Also, check the passage for evidence before accepting a strong product claim.
commonTrap.wrong: Our app is far fast than the other app.
commonTrap.correct: Our app is far faster than the other app. Look for a test or example that supports the comparison.

content.passageTitle: A Clearer Way to Manage Team Tasks
paragraphs: At a small business meeting, product manager Lina introduces PlanBee, an app for organising team tasks. She says its value proposition is simple: teams can plan work in one place and spend less time looking for updates. Lina compares it with the company’s old system. In a test with twenty users, PlanBee loaded tasks far faster, while its calendar was only slightly easier to use.

Lina then shows how a manager assigns a task and checks its progress. The setup takes about ten minutes, and the team can keep its current email service. At $12 per user each month, PlanBee costs less than the current package, which is $18. Lina says the new plan is more cost-effective, especially for a growing team. It is also scalable, so a business can add users without changing its plan. She ends by saying that the app is not perfect for every company, but it may suit teams that want clearer task lists and a lower monthly bill.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Make Your Product Stand Out

content.summary: Write a clear product comparison by naming the product, using a comparative or superlative adjective, and explaining the benefit. Use far, much, or significantly for a large difference. Use slightly, a little, or a bit for a small difference. Use by far or easily with a superlative to make a strong claim. Support your claim with a clear reason or example.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Show a Large Difference
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + is/are + far / much / significantly + comparative adjective + than + noun
blueprintItems.example: Our new processor is far more efficient than the previous model.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Show a Small Difference
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + is/are + slightly / a little / a bit + comparative adjective + than + noun
blueprintItems.example: This speaker is slightly lighter than our older model.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Make a Strong Superlative Claim
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + is/are + by far / easily + the + superlative adjective + noun + in/on + category
blueprintItems.example: This is by far the most reliable camera in its price range.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use than after a comparative adjective when you name the other product.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The new screen is much brighter our old screen.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The new screen is much brighter than our old screen.
mechanicsRules.why: Than connects the two things in a comparison.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use the before a superlative adjective.
mechanicsRules.badExample: It is easily fastest laptop in our range.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: It is easily the fastest laptop in our range.
mechanicsRules.why: A superlative normally takes the before it.

mechanicsRules.rule: Put a full stop at the end of each complete sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The battery lasts longer than the old one
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The battery lasts longer than the old one.
mechanicsRules.why: A full stop shows the reader where a sentence ends.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Product Demos and Persuasive Value

content.summary: Show a product clearly and explain why it is useful. Compare features with phrases such as far better, slightly faster, and much more cost-effective. Give a simple example or result to support each claim.
content.audioGuidance: Speak at a steady pace and pause briefly after each important feature. Stress the comparison word, as in far BET-ter and slight-ly FAST-er. Use a falling tone for clear statements and a rising tone for friendly check-in questions.

pillars.name: Clear Comparisons
pillars.target: Stress the modifier and the key adjective
pillars.explanation: In phrases such as far better and slightly faster, make the difference easy to hear. Do not rush the modifier and adjective together.

pillars.name: Useful Evidence
pillars.target: Support product claims with a result
pillars.explanation: After you describe an advantage, add a short example, such as how much time a user saves or how many steps a task takes.

pillars.name: Natural Delivery
pillars.target: Use pauses and clear sentence endings
pillars.explanation: Pause between features. Finish statements with a calm falling tone, and use a rising tone when asking the listener a question.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Value is stressed on the first syllable, while proposition is stressed on the third.
The main stress is on the second syllable in both words.
Cost-effective is stressed at the start, while effectively is stressed on the second syllable.
The stress moves from the first syllable in scalable to the third syllable in scalability.

writing.hint: Use the pattern: product + is + a little + comparative adjective + than + other product.
targetAnswers: The new bag is a little lighter than the older bag.
This bag is a little lighter than the old one.
writing.explanation: A little before a comparative adjective shows a small difference. Answers may use different product names.

writing.instruction: Write two sentences for a product pitch. Include one strong comparison and one customer benefit.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Join the ideas with because.
practicumQuestions.promptText: The battery lasts longer. Customers can use the device all day.
practicumQuestions.hint: Explain the reason that customers can use the device all day.
targetAnswers: Customers can use the device all day because the battery lasts longer.
Because the battery lasts longer, customers can use the device all day.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Because introduces the reason for an idea.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Join the ideas with but to show a contrast.
practicumQuestions.promptText: This model is slightly heavier. It costs less.
practicumQuestions.hint: Put but between the two contrasting ideas.
targetAnswers: This model is slightly heavier, but it costs less.
practicumQuestions.explanation: But connects two ideas that are different or contrasting.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with so to show a result.
practicumQuestions.promptText: The setup is much faster, ___ customers can start using the product sooner.
practicumQuestions.hint: Choose a conjunction that introduces a result.
targetAnswers: The setup is much faster, so customers can start using the product sooner.
practicumQuestions.explanation: So introduces the result of the faster setup.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation.
practicumQuestions.promptText: our new watch is slightly thinner than the last model
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with a capital letter and finish with a full stop.
targetAnswers: Our new watch is slightly thinner than the last model.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the missing word in the comparison.
practicumQuestions.promptText: This case is much stronger the old case.
practicumQuestions.hint: Add the word used to compare two things.
targetAnswers: This case is much stronger than the old case.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use than after a comparative adjective when naming the other item.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write one sentence comparing two products with a small difference.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Compare a new bag and an older bag. Use a little and lighter.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the pattern: product + is + a little + comparative adjective + than + other product.
targetAnswers: The new bag is a little lighter than the older bag.
This bag is a little lighter than the old one.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A little before a comparative adjective shows a small difference. Answers may use different product names.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write two sentences for a product pitch. Include one strong comparison and one customer benefit.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Present a new travel speaker. Use much better than and explain why it helps travellers.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use much better than in the first sentence. Use so or because to connect the benefit.
targetAnswers: This travel speaker is much better than our old model because its battery lasts all day.
Our new travel speaker is much better than the old one, so travellers can enjoy music for longer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A clear pitch makes a comparison and connects a product feature to a customer benefit. Other correct answers are possible.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds. Tell a short story about showing a product to someone.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe a time you introduced a useful product or service to another person.
storyPoints: Say what the product or service does
Explain one feature that you demonstrated
Describe the person's reaction or the result
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I showed my colleague a new planning app, and she found it much easier to use.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ ʃəʊd maɪ ˈkɒliːɡ ə njuː ˈplænɪŋ æp ənd ʃiː faʊnd ɪt mʌtʃ ˈiːziə tə juːz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use past-tense verbs and explain the product feature in a clear order.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds and compare two products or services.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell me about two products you know. Which one offers better value, and why?
storyPoints: Name the two products or services
Compare their price, speed, or ease of use
Say which one you would choose and give a reason
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The second service is slightly more expensive, but it saves much more time.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə ˈsekənd ˈsɜːvɪs ɪz ˈslaɪtli mɔːr ɪkˈspensɪv bət ɪt seɪvz mʌtʃ mɔː taɪm/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a comparative adjective and support your choice with a simple reason.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond as the sales representative in a live call. Answer the customer's question and give one clear advantage.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Customer: What does your product help my team do?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A potential customer is hearing about your business software for the first time and wants a simple explanation of its main purpose.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a sales representative. Explain the main purpose in one or two clear sentences.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: It helps your team organise projects and see what needs to be done next.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪt helps jɔː tiːm ˈɔːɡənaɪz ˈprɒdʒekts ənd siː wɒt niːdz tə biː dʌn nekst/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Give the customer a direct answer and describe a practical benefit.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond as the sales representative. Compare your product with the customer's current tool.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Customer: Is your dashboard faster than the one we already use?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A customer wants to know whether your dashboard performs better than their current tool.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a sales representative. Use a comparative phrase and avoid making an unsupported promise.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: In our tests, it was slightly faster for common tasks.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪn aʊə tests ɪt wəz ˈslaɪtli ˈfɑːstə fə ˈkɒmən tɑːsks/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use slightly faster and connect your comparison to a clear example.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond as the sales representative. Explain how the product can offer value without calling it cheap.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Customer: Your plan costs more than our current one. Why should we consider it?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A customer is concerned about the price of a business service and wants to understand its value.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a sales representative. Mention a possible saving in time or work and use a cost comparison.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: It may cost more at first, but it can be more cost-effective if it saves your team hours each week.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪt meɪ kɒst mɔː æt fɜːst bət ɪt kən biː mɔː ˌkɒst ɪˈfektɪv ɪf ɪt seɪvz jɔː tiːm ˈaʊəz iːtʃ wiːk/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Acknowledge the price and explain how the product may provide value.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond as the sales representative. Answer both parts of the customer's question in a few sentences.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Customer: Will setup interrupt our work, and can the system support a larger team later?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A growing business is worried about changing systems and adding more users in the future.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a sales representative. Describe the setup in simple terms and explain how the service can support growth.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The setup is designed to be smooth, and the system can grow as your team adds users.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə ˈsetʌp ɪz dɪˈzaɪnd tə biː smuːð ənd ðə ˈsɪstəm kən ɡrəʊ æz jɔː tiːm ædz ˈjuːzəz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Answer both concerns clearly, using simple language about setup and growth.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say a sentence using the phrase value proposition. Then give one reason a customer might choose the product.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Use value proposition in a short sentence about a product.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Our value proposition is a reliable service that saves small businesses time.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aʊə ˈvæljuː ˌprɒpəˈzɪʃən ɪz ə rɪˈlaɪəbəl ˈsɜːvɪs ðət seɪvz smɔːl ˈbɪznəsɪz taɪm/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use value proposition to describe the main benefit a customer receives.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the idea aloud using far or slightly before a comparative adjective.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Make a comparison: This version loads quickly. The older version loads more slowly.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This version is far faster than the older one.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs ˈvɜːʃən ɪz fɑː ˈfɑːstə ðən ði ˈəʊldə wʌn/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use far to make a strong comparison, followed by a comparative adjective and than.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say cost-effective three times. Stress the first syllable in cost, then say the full sentence.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Repeat: Our plan is cost-effective for small businesses.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Our plan is cost-effective for small businesses.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aʊə plæn ɪz ˌkɒst ɪˈfektɪv fə smɔːl ˈbɪznəsɪz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Keep the first part of cost-effective clear and stress the main syllable in effective.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the statement with falling intonation. Then ask the question with rising intonation.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Practise both: The dashboard is faster. Is the dashboard faster?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The dashboard is faster. Is the dashboard faster?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə ˈdæʃbɔːd ɪz ˈfɑːstə | ɪz ðə ˈdæʃbɔːd ˈfɑːstə/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Let your voice fall at the end of the statement and rise at the end of the yes-or-no question.
